summary: Defines MIB objects for managing remote network monitoring devices, in a new version of the RMON2-MIB module. It replaces RFC 2021 and updates RFC 3273. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Little spy-cameras on a network that count the traffic. This document says how to read their counters from far away.

subtitle: The SNMP data model for probes that watch a network segment and report who is talking, to whom and in which protocols.

tldr.problem: Remote monitoring devices (probes) sit on network segments and must be configured, shared by several management stations and read remotely, even when the link to the manager is intermittent.
tldr.mechanism: The RMON2-MIB module defines nine groups of SNMP objects, from a protocol directory to application-layer host and matrix tables and user-defined history, with control tables, owner strings and row-status rules for sharing a probe.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4502 is a new version of the RMON2 MIB that obsoletes RFC 2021 and updates RFC 3273. It adds enumerations for high-capacity top-N reports and deprecates objects that lacked independent implementations.

today: RFC 4502 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2021 and updates RFC 3273. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What RMON2 Is For
sections.content:
The RMON2 MIB defines objects that provide RMON analysis up to the application layer. Remote network monitoring devices, often called monitors or probes, exist for the purpose of managing a network. Often they are stand-alone devices dedicated to this job, with one per network segment, and they may also let a network management service provider reach a geographically remote client network.

The objects are an interface between an RMON agent and an RMON management application. They are not intended for direct manipulation by humans, and the management application should handle tasks such as creating rows.

The RFC lists five goals: offline operation (the probe keeps collecting when the manager cannot reach it), proactive monitoring (it logs performance so history is available at the onset of a failure), problem detection and reporting, value added data (for example highlighting the hosts that generate the most traffic or errors) and multiple managers sharing one probe.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe is a watcher that never goes to sleep. It keeps notes while you are away and can tell you which neighbors were the noisiest.

sections.title: The Nine Groups of the MIB
sections.content:
The objects are arranged into nine groups: protocol directory, protocol distribution, address mapping, network layer host, network layer matrix, application layer host, application layer matrix, user history and probe configuration. These groups are the basic units of conformance: if a device implements a group, it must implement every object in that group. Implementations must also implement the IF-MIB.

  • The protocol directory lists the protocols the probe can decode and count, and allows entries to be added, deleted and configured.
  • The protocol distribution group collects the relative amounts of octets and packets for each protocol detected on a segment.
  • The address map group lists MAC-address to network-address bindings the probe discovered and the interface they were last seen on.
  • The host groups count traffic sent from and to each network address; the application layer host group does so by protocol.
  • The matrix groups count traffic between each pair of addresses.
  • The user history group lets a manager choose which MIB instances the probe samples over time.
  • The probe configuration group controls operating parameters of the probe.

The document also contains tables that AUGMENT tables from the original RMON MIB (RFC 2819). They add dropped-frame and last-create-time conventions, offset-based filtering relative to a protocol even when its headers have variable length, and extra filter and capture status bits for WAN and generic media. These extensions are implemented by probes that also implement RMON, and add no requirements to probes that comply only with RMON.
sections.plainLanguage: The probe's notebook has nine chapters, such as which languages it can recognize, who talks to whom, and how much each pair says. If it keeps a chapter at all, it must fill in the whole chapter.

sections.title: Controlling and Sharing a Probe
sections.content:
Most groups pair a control table, normally read-write, with one or more data tables, normally read-only. Because control parameters often describe the resulting data, many can only be changed while the control entry is not active: deactivate the entry, make the SNMP Set operations, then reactivate it. Deleting a control entry deletes its associated data entries, which is a convenient way to reclaim resources.

Probe resources are scarce, and several management stations may want them at once. Each function therefore carries an OwnerString label identifying who started it. This lets a station recognize and free resources it no longer needs, lets an operator find and negotiate with the owner, and lets an operator decide to free resources another operator reserved. A device or administrator that sets up long-lived defaults marks them with an owner string starting with monitor, and stations should only modify those under the administrator's direction.

Before creating a new function, a station is encouraged to scan the control table for an instance with similar parameters to share. Rows owned by the monitor are the most trustworthy, while a row owned by another application may be modified or deleted at its discretion.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone shares the same watcher, so each request gets a name tag. That way people know whose request is whose and can ask the owner to give it up when the watcher gets overloaded.

sections.title: Adding Rows Without Collisions
sections.content:
New rows are added with the RowStatus textual convention. The agent must check the parameters against the restrictions in the MIB and against its own limits, such as lack of resources. It can do that when each parameter is set or when the row status is set to active. The RFC prefers the former wherever possible, because if the check waits until activation, the manager cannot tell which parameter caused the badValue error.

When two managers try to create the same row at once, the status object arbitrates: if it already exists, an error is returned, so only the first creator succeeds. A manager picks the row index itself, for example at random or by scanning for the first unused index, and the agent must allow a row to be created with any unused index value if it has the resources. Dangling references between tables are generally allowed, and there is no defined order for creating or deleting entries.
sections.plainLanguage: If two kids grab the same empty seat at the same moment, only the first one gets it and the other is told it is taken, so they can pick another seat.

sections.title: RMON2 Conventions
sections.content:
RMON2 uses "application level" loosely. It does not typically mean OSI Layer 7. It names a class of protocols that goes beyond MAC and network layers to include transport, session, presentation and application protocols.

The protocol directory has a notion of limited extensibility. Protocols are detected by static software written at implementation time, so a probe cannot suddenly learn to parse a new packet type. But if the code knows where the demultiplexing field is and decodes the next layer up from a table, a manager can extend it one level higher. The RFC's example: a probe configured to recognize UDP port 161 as SNMP, port 53 as DNS and port 69 as TFTP could be given a new table entry to recognize UDP port 123 as NTP and start counting those packets. Implementations may allow or disallow this for any protocol with child protocols.

Packets with link-level errors are not counted anywhere in this MIB. Packets with protocol errors are counted for all protocols below the layer where the error was found, so a network-layer error means the packet is not counted at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The watcher can only recognize the kinds of traffic it was built to know. But if it already knows the street, you can teach it about a new house on that street, though not a whole new city.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A probe must capture all packets on its local network, including packets between third parties, and analyze them for addresses, protocol usage and conversation statistics. That data may be sensitive, so administrators may wish to restrict SNMP access to the probe. Probes often also implement RMON, which can return the contents of captured packets, potentially including passwords, and the RFC recommends restricting SNMP access to those functions.

The user history group samples variables on a manager's request and stores them elsewhere, where the access control may differ. The agent MUST ensure usrHistoryObjectVariable is not writable in MIB views that do not already have read access to the entire agent, and SHOULD check access control on every sample because configuration can change over time.

Read-write and read-create objects can harm network operations if SET is allowed in a non-secure environment, and readable objects may also be sensitive. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementers are urged to use SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and operators must configure access so only principals with legitimate rights can GET or SET the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A watcher that sees every passing vehicle also sees what is in them. So only trusted people should be allowed to ask it questions or change its settings.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2021 and the TimeFilter
sections.content:
This version adds 2 new enumerations to nlMatrixTopNControlRateBase and 4 to alMatrixTopNControlRateBase, which support high-capacity top-N reports in the High Capacity RMON MIB (RFC 3273). It deprecates objects that did not have enough independent implementations to meet Draft Standard requirements: the probe download objects, the serial and serial connection configuration objects, the network configuration objects, the trap destination objects and several dropped-frames and create-time objects for Token Ring. It also fixes two SMIv2 errors, adds ranges to a number of objects to document existing practice, and updates the TimeFilter convention so that a MIB walk behaves well even for applications that do not know about it.

The TimeFilter lets a manager retrieve only the rows that changed since a given time, usually the previous poll, which cuts the SNMP transactions needed to update a table. It is not a history mechanism: it returns current values, and deleted rows cannot be detected. The appendix gives implementation notes for agents.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition adds a few new features, retires some settings nobody ever built, and offers a trick for asking only what changed since you last checked.
